Since all the questions are the same, I'll answer them here:

1) When is the bottom in? 

Obviously nobody knows. When everyone on margin is liquidated, maybe 🌝

2) Are you selling everything? 

Of course not. It's time to massively buy here. The time to sell was if you saw it coming or while it happened and if you understood early what the magnitude would be. Prices now are getting so low that in the long term returns will be crazy good. Doesn't mean we can't go much lower in the short term. But selling here is way to risky for me.

3) How did you trade this?

I didn't. I completely missed this one and am bagholding bad over the last 2 months like almost everyone else. I got complacent. Will talk about the mistakes I made and what I learned from it in the Substack post later today.

4) Are we cooked?

No. If you got margin called or did other gambles like short dated options, 3x ETFs etc - yeah your money is gone. If you're just holding long and strong we're completely fine. This deleveraging and liquidity issue doesn't break the thesis for AI hyperbulls at all! The gains over multiple years will still be generational.

5) When will we reach new ATH?

"Years?! WTF when are we up again?"

Obviously I have no clue when liquidity could improve. I don't know when the Iran war will end or what the FED will do. This crash felt entirely preventable and to some degree intentionally made. I think it could easily take until H2 2027 to reach new ATH. Not the timeline we all wanted, but better get comfortable that we now might be bagholding for quite a while. We need liquidity and macro will dictate our timeline.

In general my advice to stay sane is to simply look at a longer 3-5 year time horizon. Do you really think ANY macro can prevent stocks from ripping up again over that time horizon? The real winners will not stay this cheap for that long.

So the only people I think will stay bagholders are the ones who got liquidated or keep holding the shitcos that go bankrupt or won't recover because their earnings will keep disappointing.

On Anthropic’s first day of trading, the way they handled things was truly disgraceful.

The initial offering price was originally set at $70–$78, but it was raised straight to $83. Not only did they raise the price, but they also increased the number of shares offered from the planned 820 million to 980 million—a jump of nearly 20%.

At least with instant noodles, they usually offer more for the same price—but Anthropic went and did both: increasing the quantity and the price.

Even more outrageous is that on the very first day of trading, management cashed out $2 billion.

Are they really that desperate? They could at least put on a show—don’t rush to cash out right after going public. How are retail investors supposed not to be scared by that?

And that’s not all.

Reportedly, 10% of employee stock options were unlocked on the first day of trading—amounting to approximately 300 million shares, equivalent to nearly one-third of the total offering.

What’s truly hair-raising is the unlocking schedule that follows.

BP has been a pain in the ass for Kosmos, Mauritania and Senegal: the GTA partnership. First, the cost overruns and delays are attributed solely to BP, leaving Mauritania and Senegal furious and prompting them to launch an audit of the project costs. Following the audit, Senegalese Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko criticised the GTA contract as "one-sided and unfair" in a March 2026 televised address, as Senegal weighed legal options and contract renegotiations. Moreover, back in 2020, BP signed the marketing agreement at a very profitable rate, while the economics of the GTA partnership are less attractive, at least until 2033, when the gas contract ends and the GTA group can choose to extend it or find another offtaker on better terms. The reality is that BP built the foundations, but its inability to increase production—due to poor relations with the government and a loss of focus—is undermining the project’s economics. However, BP has not supported the idea, as its focus has been elsewhere.

In summary, BP is a forced seller because of its poor historical management of the project. This is a very interesting asset for Middle Eastern players looking to diversify their gas production, especially after the Hormuz problems. It has high-quality gas, is very close to Europe, and offers huge reserves and development potential. quoted.text:
Some fun: When has the market looked like this before?

I took the current cross-asset regime — equities, rates, credit, FX, commodities and volatility — and compared it with historical 63-trading-day periods based on both the direction and magnitude of market moves.

The closest historical match to November 2026?

April 2005 — 81% similarity.

What I found especially interesting is that it passes the macro smell test as well. Both periods combine relatively strong growth, elevated inflation, restrictive/tightening conditions, a fairly flat positive yield curve and credit markets that are not signaling acute stress.

That does not mean 2026 = 2005. There are some very important differences, particularly around housing and equity valuations.

So I also looked at what happened after the closest historical regimes.

Across the closest analogues, the median S&P 500 path was:

+2.0% after 1 month
+5.7% after 3 months
+3.4% after 6 months
+11.6% after 12 months
But the individual paths vary enormously — which is really the point.

Historical analogues aren't forecasts. They are a way of asking: when markets have been pricing a similar combination of growth, inflation, rates, credit and risk before, what happened next?

Still experimenting with this, but I think there is something pretty interesting here.

Over the past couple weeks we've met with management teams across memory, optics, neoclouds, semis, semi cap equipment and substrates.

Everyone is frustrated and confused about their stock prices but everyone is still very, very bullish.

Everyone expects 2027 capex to be significantly higher than 2026 and they expect 2028 capex to be moderately to significantly higher than 2027. 

Everyone knows the YoY capex growth rates will decelerate but the total dollars spent will continue to get bigger... at least for the next few years. Everyone says we're still in the early innings of ai adoption. 

Every company in the ai ecosystem is 50-100% sold out for 2027 and 40-80% sold out for 2028. 

Everyone is sitting on LTAs from the hyperscalers... some of those LTAs are getting signed and they last anywhere from 3 years to 6+ years... and they're getting done at record prices and record margins. Customers can't take the chance of not having enough supply to meet their needs over the next 3-5 years... locking up supply at record prices is better than not having enough supply when it's needed the most. 

Some of these LTAs could consume more than 50% of their supply over the next 2-3 years and at least one company has an LTA that would consume 75% of their capacity over the next 2-3 years. 

Neoclouds continue to see demand that is 5-10x higher than capacity. Many of them are saying the financing concerns are overblown. They're seeing 3-5 year deals get signed at 10-20% higher prices that the first half of 2026 and they think deals signed in the first half of 2027 will have 10-20% higher prices than deals signed in the second half of 2026. Power is still a big bottleneck and many sites are dealing with small construction delays but nothing is getting canceled. Customers are desperate for compute. Many of the neoclouds are trying to reserve 10-15% of capacity for shorter term deals and spot market because rates are 2-3x higher than the 3-5 year deals. 

Memory companies say demand will outstrip supply until 2029 at the earliest. They are very confident LTAs won't get cancelled because even at record prices for memory, the customers have enough margin to make it work. 

I know there's lots of fear and uncertainty in the market right now but it's not showing up in the demand... it remains stronger than ever... many backlogs are growing faster than current revenues.

In 20+ years of investing, I've honestly never seen this much dislocation between fundamentals and valuations. This is truly a historic time to be an investor and not in a good way. It's very hard to be patient and lean into your conviction/thesis during times like this but that's probably the right strategy for most long-term investors. 

Hopefully the lows are near. Make sure you are getting sleep, sunlight and exercise. Protect your mental health if possible.

One of the first things employees heard at the staff meeting the next day was that they’d get their performance ratings and find out the size of their stock grants in December. My friend also told me about a question someone asked Jonah Alben, NVIDIA’s senior vice president of GPU engineering, at a meeting with their whole team. The employee said several outside recruiters had been reaching out pretty aggressively and asked whether NVIDIA had a plan to keep people from being poached.

The answer was about what you’d expect. But hearing that someone had asked the question gave me a sense of just how much attention NVIDIA’s senior engineers are getting from recruiters, especially those at the director level and above. People with that kind of experience are hard to find in Silicon Valley right now.

My friend is worried Jensen Huang might not come back. They wonder what the next few years will look like for NVIDIA. They only joined recently, but they said a lot of the excitement they felt when they took the job is already gone.

NVIDIA offered them less in total compensation than its competitors did. They chose NVIDIA anyway because they believed in Jensen and in the company’s future under him. Yesterday they told me they regret that decision. I tried to reassure them and told them I thought things would get better….

posts.name: Aidan Mackenzie
posts.text:
The Senate passing permitting is absolutely historic! Let's take a second to remember how long folks have been trying to get major permitting & transmission reforms: 🧵

For 50 years presidents have been frustrated by slow permitting and wanted to expand the grid. But for decades environmental and utility opposition made reform impossible

– 1971: Nixon asked Congress to reform transmission. But Congress never voted on the proposal (environmental and state's rights concerns blocked it)

– 1979: President Carter tried to get reforms to speed up energy approvals and judicial review to fix "endless roadblocks." Environmentalists opposed and the bill died in the House in 1980

– 2001: President Bush sought reforms for transmission developers to acquire land (Congress delayed until 2005)

– 2005: Following a massive blackout in 2003, Congress finally acted to boost grid development In the Energy Policy Act of 2005. However, the bill was change to add language that undercut the federal backstop for transmission (the process never built any lines)

– 2009: Obama asked Congress to facilitate building out the grid but Congress's proposal to give FERC siting authority never passed (utilities and environmental groups opposed)

– 2011: After permitting slowed economic recovery projects Obama said "Shovel-ready was not as shovel-ready as we expected"

– 2011-2024: FERC attempted to act to facilitate new interregional lines. However, FERC Order 1000 has failed to produce even a single line

– 2015: Congress passed the FAST Act, which created FAST-41. But Congress declined to add major reforms to judicial review or touch the underlying permitting laws

– 2018: Trump's request to limit reviews to 2 years was never taken up by Congress

– 2022: Despite ongoing delays to infrastructure and climate projects, the Senate voted down the Manchin-Biden-Schumer permitting reform & transmission proposal (Opposition from environmentalists and transmission opponents)

– 2023: Congress declined to include major reforms in the Fiscal Responsibility Act (added only very minor changes)

– 2024: The Manchin-Barrasso bipartisan permitting & transmission bill never got a floor vote

The reforms in BAAJA are transformative and historic. This Congress is on the cusp of reform that has been impassive for over 50 years

quoted.text:
Ok, I’m going to be as polite as possible even though I’m tired of explaining this. Forward earnings are horrible for assessing valuations when we’re at the end of the cycle.

Analysts extrapolate recent growth and elevated profit margins instead of anticipating mean reversion or recessionary contractions. As a result, the denominator in forward price to earnings ratios stay artificially high while the business cycle is already turning, making valuations appear more reasonable than trailing or cyclically adjusted ratios.

Students of financial history understand this. During the GFC, actual earnings collapsed about 92%, yet consensus estimates only fell about 6%. This disconnect happens at the end of every cycle and the beginning of every recession (although the GFC is an extreme example). Downward revisions to estimates only come after the damage is already visible.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Productivity, Not Rate Hikes, Tames Supercore!

Supercore inflation is no mystery, and it’s not a story about the federal funds rate. It is unit labor costs: pay minus productivity.

PCE supercore and nonfarm unit labor costs have a correlation of 0.82 since 1960, and 0.91 on two-year averages. In 2022, productivity fell 1.5%, unit labour costs rose 5.3%, and supercore peaked at 5.3% in October. In 2024, productivity rose 3.1% and unit labor  costs slowed to 2.0%, even as pay grew 5.1%. 

Supercore came down. The 1996 to 2004 boom worked the same way: productivity 3.1%, pay 4.4%, unit labor costs 1.3%, supercore 2.6%.

The only extended stretch when supercore held near 2% was post-GFC secular stagnation, from mid-2009 to early 2020. It averaged 2.1% and stayed in a 1.5% to 2.5% band in 82% of months, against 15% otherwise. It got there through weak pay of 2.5%, not a productivity boom.

Supercore has been above 2% in 88% of months since 1960, with a long-run average of 4.05%. It was 3.6% in September 2026. In the third quarter, unit labour costs were 2.4%, productivity 2.1% and pay 4.5%. Rate hikes do not create productivity. They cut the investment, including AI capex, that does.

A Fed that hikes into a productivity boom to chase a 2% supercore it has seen only in secular stagnation is not following the data. It is going rogue. The Fed should protect the productivity cycle, not choke it.

posts.text:
Coup de tonnerre énorme dans les mathématiques

Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, a publié ce vendredi une note sur son site perso. 

Première phrase : « I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis »

Et il va plus loin dans la note la même méthode réglerait aussi l'hypothèse de Riemann généralisée

Pour l'échelle, elle a été posée par Bernhard Riemann en 1859. Ça fait 167 ans que les plus grands mathématiciens se cassent les dents dessus

Si ça tient, c'est une news énormissime pour le monde des maths. Historique total

1. C'est quoi l'hypothèse de Riemann ?

Les nombres premiers (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13…) ont l'air de tomber au hasard sur la droite des nombres

Riemann a trouvé une fonction, la fonction zêta, qui encode leur répartition. Elle s'annule en une infinité de points, ses « zéros »

L'hypothèse dit que tous les zéros intéressants (les non triviaux) sont alignés sur une seule et même droite, celle où la partie réelle vaut 1/2

En clair : les nombres premiers sont aussi bien rangés qu'ils peuvent l'être. Le désordre apparent cache un ordre quasi parfait

C'est l'un des 7 problèmes du millénaire du Clay Institute, avec 1 million de dollars à la clé. À ce jour, un seul a été officiellement résolu : la conjecture de Poincaré, par Perelman

2. La boîte de Pandore des maths est ouverte

Des milliers de théorèmes commencent par « si l'hypothèse de Riemann est vraie, alors… »

Des générations de mathématiciens ont construit des étages entiers sur ces fondations sans savoir si elles tenaient

Si la preuve est validée, tous ces résultats deviennent vrais d'un coup. Et la version généralisée en débloque encore plus

Et je vous vois venir sur la crypto, une preuve ne casse pas RSA. Le chiffrement repose sur la difficulté de factoriser de très grands nombres, et savoir où sont les zéros ne donne aucune méthode pour le faire donc safe pour la cryptographie

3. Comment il l'a fait

Il n'y a pas de papier. Toute la preuve est publiée en Lean, le langage qui permet à un ordinateur de vérifier chaque étape, découpée en 14 archives

Il crédite Claude de plusieurs étapes clés et dit que le modèle l'a largement dépassé vers la fin. Une version lisible par un humain est promise plus tardx je pense ce soir

Alpöge a déjà un sacré palmarès cette année, voir même délirant, c'est lui qui avait réfuté la conjecture jacobienne avec Claude en juillet

4. Pourquoi il faut rester prudent

Pour l'instant, c'est une annonce. Personne en dehors de son cercle n'a encore confirmé que le code compile, ni que le théorème final dit exactement ce que dit l'hypothèse de Riemann

La communauté va tout télécharger et vérifier. Si le Lean passe, le problème serait réglé sur le plan formel avant même qu'on comprenne la preuve, une première pour un problème de ce niveau

Et le timing est hilarant encore, note sort au lendemain de l'IPO d'Anthropic, quand il faut aider le prix à monter après une première journée difficile, Il en parle lui-même dans le texte et assure que la lecture cynique est fausse

5. Elles vont toutes tomber

En octobre, OpenAI avait déjà prouvé la « quasi-hypothèse de Riemann » : une bande entière sans zéros. Alex Kontorovich (Rutgers) disait que ça vaudrait une médaille Fields instantanée si un humain l'avait fait

Terence Tao le résume très bien : on est passé de la rareté des preuves à leur abondance, et la « monnaie » des problèmes du millénaire a été « basically hyperinflated »

Yang-Mills à moitié, Navier-Stokes annoncé mais toujours contesté, et maintenant Riemann sur la table

Je vous le disais, les grands problèmes ouverts vont tomber les uns après les autres
